opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think there's a real gap right now in how we think about AI safety. A lot of the public conversation, and a lot of the published research, focuses on general-purpose harms: toxicity, bias, weapons-related misuse, jailbreaks. Those matter, but when you deploy a model in a specific domain like finance, law, or healthcare, the risks look quite different. In financial services, for example, you worry about a model giving something that reads like investment advice, leaking confidential information, or producing content that runs into regulatory issues. Most general safety taxonomies and guardrail systems simply don't cover those categories, and when we've looked closely, off-the-shelf guardrails often miss them.

Academics are well positioned for a few reasons. The first is depth of expertise. Universities have people who've spent careers studying how a legal system or a medical practice actually works, where the failure modes are, and what the stakes are. Combining that with NLP and evaluation expertise is exactly what you need to build a meaningful risk taxonomy for a domain, rather than just porting over a generic one.

The second is independence. A company deploying a system has incentives, even well-intentioned ones, that shape what it measures and publishes. Academic researchers can take a more neutral look, publish negative results, and say "this whole category of risk is being ignored" without a product roadmap attached.

The third is that you don't need frontier-scale compute to do this work well. Much of the most valuable safety research in specialized domains is about careful problem definition: building taxonomies, collecting realistic data, designing evaluations that reflect how practitioners actually use these tools, and red-teaming with domain knowledge. That's careful, interdisciplinary, methodological work, which is exactly what academia does well, and it doesn't require training a giant model from scratch.

Finally, there's a public-good aspect. Benchmarks, taxonomies, and evaluation frameworks benefit everyone when they're open, and academia has the norms to make them open. So I'd really encourage academic groups to partner with domain experts and pick a vertical they care about. There's a lot of low-hanging and very impactful work to be done there.

r001.rationale: The response calls specialized-domain AI safety a real gap and says general taxonomies miss domain-specific risks.

r002.rationale: It says universities have people with deep expertise in fields such as law and medicine, which can be combined with NLP and evaluation expertise.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a couple of reasons for this. The first one is just where the knowledge actually lives. When we talk about something like financial services, or healthcare, or law, the risks that matter are extremely specific to that domain. A general-purpose safety benchmark will ask whether a model refuses to help with something obviously harmful, but it won't ask whether a model gives advice that's subtly non-compliant with a particular regulation, or whether it misreads a contract clause in a way that a practitioner would immediately catch. The people who understand those failure modes deeply are often not sitting inside AI labs. They're in business schools, law schools, medical schools, and the social sciences, and they've spent years studying how these systems of rules and incentives actually work.

The second reason is independence. If I'm building a model inside a company, I have a very natural incentive to evaluate it in ways that make it look good, or at least to focus on the risks that are most relevant to my product. Academics don't have that pressure in the same way. They can ask uncomfortable questions, they can publish negative results, and they can take the time to build a careful evaluation without worrying about a release deadline. That makes their findings more credible, and it also means they'll look in places industry simply wouldn't think to look.

And the third thing, which I think is underappreciated, is that a lot of the safety research people in the specialized domains have the right methodological toolkit already. If you look at how economists or psychologists design experiments, they're very careful about confounders, about validity, about whether a measurement actually captures the construct they care about. A lot of AI evaluation today is honestly pretty sloppy by those standards. So bringing in researchers who have that rigor, and pairing it with domain expertise, is where I think some of the most valuable safety work is going to come from.

The caveat is that it requires access. You need model access, you need compute, and you often need some collaboration with people who understand the systems from the inside. So part of what I'm interested in is how we lower those barriers, so that the people who are best positioned to find these risks are actually able to do the work.

r001.rationale: The response says general safety benchmarks miss domain-specific risks and that industry may not look for them, presenting specialized-domain AI safety as an overlooked research area.

r002.rationale: The response says domain expertise often resides in academic fields and describes pairing safety work with domain expertise, but it does not say academics have access to subject matter experts.

astra-6.text:
I think academics are in a good position because they bring deep expertise in particular domains. If you want to understand how an AI system might cause harm in medicine, for example, you need people who understand medicine and the context in which that system would be used. You can’t necessarily identify those risks just by knowing how to build a language model.

Universities bring those different kinds of expertise together. There’s an opportunity for AI researchers to collaborate with people who can ask, “What would a failure look like in my field? What are the consequences, and how would we test for that?” Academics can also pursue those questions independently of the pressure to ship a particular product. That makes them valuable for identifying risks that a general-purpose evaluation might miss.

r001.rationale: The response describes specialized-domain risks that general-purpose evaluations might miss, but does not say this intersection is underresearched.

r002.rationale: It says universities bring different expertise together and describes AI researchers collaborating with people who understand the relevant field.

sol-6.1.text:
I think academics are in a good position because they have deep expertise in particular domains, and that expertise is really important for understanding what can go wrong. If you’re evaluating a model in a medical context, for example, you need people who understand medicine to help identify which mistakes are consequential and whether your evaluation actually captures those risks.

Universities also bring together people from different disciplines. You can have machine learning researchers working with domain experts to turn a broad concern about safety into concrete research questions: What are the possible harms? Under what conditions do they arise? And how would we know whether a mitigation works? That’s a place where academics can make a valuable contribution.

r001.rationale: The response describes domain-specific AI safety research and its value, but does not say this area is underresearched.

r002.rationale: It says universities bring together machine learning researchers and domain experts, supporting the claim that academics can access subject matter expertise.
